questions.q: Why does a brand-new correlation rule typically fire more often than expected when first deployed?
options: Real environments are messier than the clean example used to design the rule — service accounts, scheduled jobs, and ordinary mistakes don't match the textbook pattern cleanly
New rules can only ever be tested in a lab, never in production
New rules are always written with a 0% threshold by default
SIEMs disable tuning for the first 24 hours automatically
questions.explain: A rule built from a clean example can't yet distinguish real attack behavior from ordinary operational noise.

questions.q: What are the two main kinds of changes tuning usually involves?
options: Changing the SIEM vendor and migrating all data
Disabling logging for the affected accounts
Deleting the rule and rewriting it from scratch each time
Adjusting thresholds and adding exclusions for known-benign sources
questions.explain: Tuning typically means tightening the threshold/time window or explicitly excluding a confirmed-benign source.

questions.q: In the backup service account example, why is adding an exclusion the better fix rather than raising the threshold for everyone?
options: Raising the threshold for everyone would also make the rule less sensitive to real attacks, while an exclusion only silences the one confirmed-benign, already-investigated source
Raising a threshold is technically impossible once a rule is deployed
Exclusions are required by every SIEM vendor's licensing terms
There is no difference between the two approaches
questions.explain: An exclusion targets the specific known-benign source without weakening the rule's sensitivity everywhere else.

questions.q: Why is alert fatigue described as a genuine security risk rather than just an inconvenience?
options: It causes SIEM software to crash under high alert volume
Analysts who repeatedly dismiss the same false positive become measurably more likely to under-investigate future alerts from that rule, including true ones
It only affects how dashboards look, not analyst behavior
It has no documented effect on investigation quality
questions.explain: The habit of dismissing noise from an untuned rule doesn't turn off selectively, even on the night a real attack occurs.

questions.q: Why is tuning described as an ongoing process rather than a one-time task?
options: SIEMs automatically re-tune every rule without analyst input
Tuning is only legally required once per year
Once tuned, a rule's thresholds can never be changed again
A rule that's well-tuned today can get noisy again as new service accounts or scheduled tasks change the environment, so SOCs revisit false-positive rates on a recurring basis
questions.explain: Environments keep changing, so a rule's false-positive rate needs periodic review, not a single fix-and-forget pass.
